title: For those who have seen Godzilla Minus One, why do you like it?

commenti.body: [removed]

What I most appreciated was the documentation of a pair of two people from the rubble of post-war to a semblance of normalcy (and then obviously right back to rubble).

I was in a theater where literally EVERY single dramatic scene was interrupted by a small group of teens mocking the melodrama. For the first time in my life I shouted in the middle of a movie for them to stfu. So my coverage of those scenes is quite tinted, however I did appreciate them in the same vein of Train to Busan. It could be seen as cheesy, but the dialogue was purposeful and lead towards a very particular conclusion (pretty much everything leading up to him feeling the need to make a sacrifice, and then realizing that there's more than one way, and he need not do what he was told).

The one bit of dialogue I found unforgivably cheesy was his friend who did nothing but push for him to marry the girl and treat her better. His dialogue felt "Marvel-esque" but in the long run he was the only person pushing the standard "get married" agenda in the whole movie so I forgave it.

Honestly, I'd have been happy with a movie just of the human story with no Godzilla. Recovering from being on the losing side of such a massive and traumatic war isn't a perspective we see very often, and I found it really heartening.
Sorry about those teens. That sucks. I’m glad you still found some enjoyment from the film!
I also enjoyed the film being more civilian oriented.
Im with you. Godzilla movies have set an extremely low bar for what is considered quality when a movie like this garners so much praise. It may have had a tight script but it’s still cheesy as hell.

I think it’s rather hard to make monster movies at such a large scale. Alien invasion, Godzilla, King Kong, pacific rim. It’s very hard to get creative because it’s quite obvious what the progression is. Freak out, destruction, “let’s get rid of the threat.” 

I did enjoy this being more of a character driven film, but I just don’t think it was done well. A bit sad because I really liked everything about Godzilla.

I’m kind of with you. I like the ideas. But I thought the movie was too short on Godzilla. Even the big city destruction scene felt too brief and almost nonsensical to me. Like how he’s away from the train then suddenly at the train and picking it up for no real reason other than Noriko was on it. 

And then when he finally does do the breath attack, we don’t really sit with that. He just fucks off. And it’s never really made all that clear why he went to shore anyway. 

It felt forced rather than earned. And wasn’t as harrowing as the original or even Shin. Though people will definitely disagree with that. I just thought those movies sat us in the devastation in a far more powerful way.

Then I liked the human story. Until the end when the tone switched to a Shonen anime. Everyone started to feel like caricatures rather than the characters they were. Especially with the absurd tug boat scene. That pretty much broke my suspension of disbelief.

the director of this Godzilla is famous for a film series called "Always - Sunset on Third Street" that takes place in 1950s Tokyo. it's nostalgic and sentimental. that's the mood he favors. this movie is called "Minus One" but it goes from minus to plus pretty smoothly: our pilot finds a job and a crew and a family without much trouble.

the crazy fantasy of the film is not just the kaiju but the fact that all forms of authority (the Japanese goverment and the occupying American forces) just check out as an existential threat rampages. Godzilla makes landfall at Ginza, just a 10-minute walk from where Gen. MacArthur has set up his HQ... but not one American soldier in sight.

volunteers end up taking care of the problem of Godzilla. it's one fantasy makeover of the sorrows of postwar recovery.

Yes!! This is better said than I could put it. It felt very forced. That’s what I meant when it feels like we were just being pulled along to the movie. Like someone speedrunning us through a museum… “and this is Godzilla… oh and these are our characters… now we have to run over here to show you the moral struggle.” Also… it was so funny when they had him at the *deepest part of the bay* and Godzilla is *standing upright* and then you see his legs move as if he is walking.

I've never liked the "added nothing new" metric. It's a tightly written script with Godzilla in it. I prefer the big swing of Shin Godzilla too, but movies and art aren't a rat race for new ideas.

I know we're on TrueFilm, but this is a blockbuster movie. Few to no Godzilla films (maybe Shin) have ever aimed at Gojira '54's legacy. 


To the lightheartedness: the film skips 2 years to a "light hearted tone" during the so far successful rebuilding of Japan. The trauma is there, but they're supposed to be hopeful until Godzilla shows up. I agree all of the Godzilla despair seems to be contained in only one sequence - but that's where the movie decides to be about triumph, not tragedy. 

To each their own, but I do take a little umbrage with calling the script "lazy." Neat, tight, by the numbers even - but not lazy.

See, and I think the premise is really cool. It just wasn’t shown well. When I heard this was post-war I was very intrigued. Then getting into the film, I realized that this is more of a character arc than a peoples’ arc.

Maybe lazy isn’t a great word. I love the adage “show, don’t tell” and so when I watch a film with dialogue that’s way too talky, a little cheesy, and practically telling us the plot, I get bored. I like learning from watching and dialogue that feels like it’s authentic.

it really felt like this movie is a fantasy redo of recovery - not just from hunger and rebuilding from the rubble but the repair of the male psyche. central to the pilot's story is his coming to terms with survival guilt and how the mechanic stops blaming him for "not doing his duty."

it's old fashioned, that's for sure. the movie can imagine a recovery without any sign of authority but it can't put a single woman into that room of brave volunteers.

I really loved the film, but I am a pretty big Goji/Kaiju geek, so of course my opinion of the film can’t be unbiased. I totally hear what people say about the plot feeling very railroad-y, the acting being a bit much, etc, but it’s also a bit of a “water in the desert” scenario. Following the Godzilla film formula historically leads to a pretty mediocre movie that’s fun if you turn your brain off (for both Toho and Legendary), but Minus One followed the formula pretty closely and was able to make an engaging film with interesting human story beats, not just destruction scenes. The hammy, trope-y acting and melodrama I chalk up to regional differences between Western and Japanese acting styles, and it also helped establish the characters better for a foreign audience that might not be able to remember or keep track of Japanese names. I definitely enjoyed the acting way more than in Shin Godzilla. The melodrama and troped I honestly didn’t mind, I don’t think the film was trying to reinvent the wheel or anything, it’s just trying to tell an interesting story through and with Godzilla. 
On the Godzilla front, I really enjoyed how much we saw of him (especially compared to 2014) and how faithful the design and movement was to the Heisei-era suit while still feeling fierce and unique. Might have taken the number one Goji design spot from Shin Goji. I think this is maybe the most “abstract” Godzilla has been as a character? Of course there’s always Goji as a symbol of nuclear fear and such, but in Minus One he’s pretty clearly Koichi’s personal demon/ptsd in a post-war world. Of course there’s the destruction and the effect Godzilla has on the world, but I think the film works a lot better when reading it through Koichi’s personal journey and him overcoming this survivor’s guilt/conflict for Godzilla to actually be defeated. 
This turned a bit ramble, but yeah happy to talk more about it!

He's not a "defeated man," he's a man who was traumatized by a horrific war and did something that's basically the most dishonorable and shameful thing you could possibly have done in Imperial Japan (chickened out and shirked his duty by not following kamikaze orders). 

Imagine coming home from war to find your parents house burned to a crisp, knowing their dead, and your neighbor instantly blaming you for it. It's hard to emphasize just how much a Japanese man would have been shamed and ostracized for his actions. Japanese soldiers almost never surrendered because the thought of going home and family, friends, and associates knowing you were a POW was worse than dying on the battlefield. That's how shameful it was. These are not themes explored in your average American blockbuster and it's not a trope I see in a lot of movies?

Was it melodramatic and a little one note? Sure. Are there more complex, emotional, psychological dramas out there? Of course. But as an American viewer I thought it was pretty cool to watch a big blockbuster, a monster movie, with awesome spectacle combined with a story that I found moving that dove deep into trauma and what it would have been like to carry that shame in imperial Japan, and what it must have been like for those people trying to build a life among the ruins of firebombed Tokyo and the national trauma/grief of having just been nuked, twice.

I agree that "nothing new here" is kind of a bad yardstick to measure a movie but like I said it's a little baffling to me to suggest we've seen this all before. At least as an American, this movie was a breath of fresh air to me and felt very different than your typical US blockbuster IMHO.

Absolutely agreed. It feels to me like a lot of people are missing some of the culture specific subtext that you mentioned, and some of the choices made at the end of the film, while predictable, still moved me deeply because of said context. 

There’s also a style of acting in Japanese films that people who are not accustomed to them might be seeing for the first time. It either works for you or it doesn’t.

Yeah after I typed out the comment I got to thinking about how I enjoyed it a lot because I've learned a bit about Imperial Japan through historical podcasts and stuff and it's really fascinating to me. Sure it was a predictable plot and in a way, it's sort of an archetypical story about a man who's ashamed of his sins "redeeming" himself, but all that cultural subtext was pretty novel for me, I personally haven't watched many blockbusters exploring the time period and what it might be like to be a kamikaze pilot with survivors guilt and bear that cross of shame, let alone a monster/genre film. Only relevant, comparable touch point I have is, well, OG Godzilla.

Yeah there’s a ton of Japanese media about the noble act of self sacrifice, and to see a Japanese movie where the message was “choose to live instead” was very moving to me. This and OG Godzilla are absolutely my favorites in the series for how they lament the loss of life.
The effects are not supposed to be chasing verisimilitude. Him wading in the bay is in homage to the visual language of pretty much every single suitmation Godzilla to date.

It sounds like you did not like the movie for all the same reasons that I absolutely loved it.

The theme of noble sacrifice rather than expendable human life was incredibly touching to me and I do think says a lot about the way that Japanese culture shifted from an empire under the Meiji Restoration into the constitution of 1947 was amazing and gave me a perspective on that history that I had never "gotten" as an American.

I also thought that the themes of information control not only in the government but in the personal interactions is a very powerful theme that is present throughout the movie. I noticed it early on, but it just kept being explored in such beautiful and moving ways.

I personally think that it is a very humanizing and humanist masterpiece. That said, I completely get why it might not be your cup of tea.

Finally, someone tells it like it is.

The movie is fine. Feels like the discourse is being driven weird fanboys (82% of the opening weekend audience was male) or people who don't ever really watch foreign films that aren't action films. There were four high profile Japanese films this year alone that are better but I guess they don't have a giant radioactive monster.

He came back from a war that simply destroyed their young men. I think it's the captain who has a line about how many young men died because of bad planning and hunger. War is hell, and it destroyed them. Godzilla is like a personification of that war. He's the PTSD and horror of war, brought back.

And the Kamikaze pilot finds a way to use his training to live, instead of dying for his country. It's a refutation of the societal need to sacrifice himself for the whole, basically a refutation of the entire war.

God this movie was good, laden with subtext, yet having some amazing monster movie parts.

Imo theres nothing wrong with using a tried and true plot formulas, especially in such a specific genre piece.  Pretty much every film after the first devolves further and further from the philosophical themes that made the original such a novel concept.  I think going back to the roots or basics is fine, and I really enjoyed the restraint and frugality they showed with all the human elements of the story so they could really make Godzilla shine.

My only complaint is I found the acting lacking in the emotional punch scenes. And I don't really blame the actors. I think they were expected to do too much with too little.  I think some better writing, and editing finesse, would have made those moments hit more on point.  But then again, this is a Kaiju flick, so I can't complain too much. Overall, a solid addition to the Reiwa era.

There’s a weird political subtext to the movie, if you interpret it in relation to Japanese history, in the WW2 era and today. 

In the decades before WW2, Japan created an empire, invading and conquering Korea, Taiwan, parts of China, many Pacific Islands. 

At the end of WW2, Japan’s defeat was total and humiliating. The empire was lost, cities destroyed by atomic bombs and firebombing, the Emperor was forced to announce the he was not divine and had erred. The USA occupied and ran Japan for 7 years, wrote a new Japanese Constitution for them, and through favorable treaties remained an outsize player in Japanese politics and economics for decades. There are USA military bases in Japan, even today. 

Godzilla Minus One is a historical fantasy that rewrites history to erase the humiliation of Japan’s WW2 defeat. 

In the movie, the Americans are completely written out. Somehow they are not interested in Godzilla. In real life, Japan was prohibited from having a military. Yet, the movie is a fantasy of Japan triumphing over an enemy through its cunning military power. At the very moment when Japan was actually at its weakest!

Skip forward to our current historical moment. Japan remains constitutionally prohibited in its military capacity, and its economy has largely stagnated since its 1980s heights. China seems to be poised to expand its borders. The USA, itself politically unstable, is an unreliable ally. 

Given all this — the film rewrites history to provide a reassuring fantasy to a Japanese audience. In the imaginary world of Godzilla Minus One, Japan remains powerful in its defeat. Japanese people remain unified and and able to govern themselves. Through their technical ingenuity and extreme courage, Japan is able to defeat even the most powerful and aggressive enemy. 

None of this was true in 1945-47. And it’s still not true today. 

I didn’t even get to the part about how the film glorifies the figure of the Kamikaze. But, the film really represents a return to Japan’s pre-1945 ideas about itself. 

TLDR: the film rewrites history to present a vision of Japan that tries to erase Japan’s WW2 defeat. This is politically kinda weird, and says a lot about Japan’s current hopes and fears.

Because the story isn’t about Godzilla. There are two types of Godzilla movies. The ones that are extremely cartoonish where it’s Godzilla battling Mothra. Or some stories where it focuses more on the characters developing around a “what if a massive dinosaur attacked our city”

You also have to remember that a lot of this movie was an homage to the originals. They easily could have made a stable walking dinosaur. But they decided on the slow robotic movement. 

They could have had a realistic dinosaur, each scale in detail. But they decided on going with the original design and remaster it. 

So maybe change your paradigm. Then rewatch it. Maybe it might show you a new perspective.
